sections.title: What it is
sections.content: Older Hungarian had a true passive: the verb takes `-atik/-etik` or `-tatik/-tetik`, on the same pattern as the causative `-at/-et`, `-tat/-tet`. *Követel* becomes *követeltetik* ('is demanded'), *tilt* becomes *tiltatik* ('is forbidden'), *elutasít* becomes *elutasíttatik* ('is rejected'). The past adds `-ott/-ett`: *elutasíttatott* ('was rejected'). You will meet it in 19th-century laws, old factory and guild rules, and the Károli Bible (*Kérjetek és adatik néktek*, 'Ask, and it shall be given you').

sections.title: Old documents → modern Hungarian
rows: A munkástól feltétlen engedelmességet követelnek. (Unconditional obedience is demanded of the worker.)
A munkaidő alatt a beszélgetés tiltatik.
Munkaidő alatt tilos beszélgetni. (Talking is forbidden during working hours.)
A béremelési kérelmet elutasították. (The pay-rise request was rejected.)
A rendtartást minden műhelyben kifüggesztik. (The rules are posted in every workshop.)

sections.title: What modern Hungarian uses instead
sections.content: Modern Hungarian has no everyday passive. For 'something is done' it uses the active verb in the third person plural with no subject: *elutasították* ('they rejected it', that is, 'it was rejected'). Rules are stated with *tilos* or *kötelező* plus an infinitive: *tilos beszélgetni*. A resulting state uses the *-va/-ve* form with *van*: *a kérelem el van utasítva*.

Read the *-tatik* passive, but don't write it in a modern text: today it sounds archaic or mock-solemn, and a workplace notice written in it reads as a parody of officialese. Don't add *által* to name who did it, either: *a vezetőség által elutasíttatott* is a calque. Say *a vezetőség elutasította*. A few forms survive as set phrases: *ha megadatik* ('if one is granted the chance'), *nem adatott meg neki* ('it was not granted to him').
